To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) in an expanding universe the perturbed Einstein equations are most simply written in terms of energy-density perturbations on constant-curvature hypersurfaces; (ii) the conserved quantity on large scales in an expanding flat universe is the fractional, spatial density gradient on hypersurfaces with constant expansion, and that (iii) the perturbation dynamics on large scales in nonflat universes is most suitably formulated in terms of the energy density perturbation on constant-curvature surfaces.

the conserved perturbation quantity on scales larger than H-1 is proportional to the spatial gradient of the fractional, energy density perturbation on hypersurfaces where the expansion is constant, or, alternatively, proportional to the expansion or the curvature perturbation on hypersufraces where the energy density is constant.
the conserved perturbation quantity on large scales is the fractional spatial gradient of energy density, which is the same quantity that is conserved in Newtonian gravity.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in the large-scale and weak-perturbation limits the energy density perturbation is the only quantity which is conservatively coupled to the background expansion and curvature.
the linear cosmological perturbations are described by a single conserved quantity on scales larger than H^{-1}.

the perturbation dynamics of the large-scale limit is described by the evolution of the fractional, comoving energy density gradient, or by the evolution of expansion and curvature perturbation variables, on hypersurfaces with constant energy density, constant expansion or constant curvature, respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the perturbation theory of the linear cosmological perturbations is simplified by the introduction of new covariant and physically meaningful variables.

the linear cosmological perturbations on large scales can be described by the evolution of a single variable, the fractional energy density perturbation on hypersurfaces with constant energy density, or equivalently on hypersurfaces whose curvature is constant in the absence of anisotropic stress.

the large-scale limit is most naturally described by a set of variables which are conserved and which are related to the fractional, spatial gradients of the energy density and the velocity divergence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for the linear theory in the large-scale, flat background limit, the perturbation variables are not only conserved but also have physical meaning on constant expansion hypersurface.
the perturbation theory of the large-scale limit is much simpler than the full perturbation theory of a spatially flat universe.
, in the limit of large scales, the perturbation dynamics can be described by means of a few conserved variables which are related to the perturbations of the energy density, expansion and curvature.
